note.explanation: Domain Eukarya contains four kingdoms in this section: Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia. They differ in how their members are organised, obtain food, and in the materials of their cell walls.
note.simple: To identify a eukaryote's kingdom, check whether it is unicellular or multicellular, how it gets food, and whether it has a cell wall—and what that wall is made of.
note.checkQuestion: To which kingdom does yeast belong?
note.title: The four kingdoms of Domain Eukarya
steps: Protista includes unicellular, colonial, filamentous or simple multicellular eukaryotes.
Fungi absorb food from decaying matter and have cell walls made of chitin.
Plantae are multicellular autotrophs with cellulose cell walls.
Animalia are multicellular heterotrophs that ingest food and have no cell walls.
note.answer: The four kingdoms are Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia.

modelAnswer: Kingdom Protista includes eukaryotes which are unicellular or colonial or filamentous or simple multicellular.
Plant-like protists are autotrophs; animal-like protists are heterotrophs, and fungus-like protists absorb nutrients from decaying organic matter.
Kingdom Fungi consists of heterotrophic eukaryotes with cell walls made of chitin; they absorb food from decaying matter.
Kingdom Plantae includes multicellular autotrophs with cell walls made of cellulose; they prepare food through photosynthesis.
Kingdom Animalia includes multicellular heterotrophs that ingest food and digest it within their bodies; they have no cell walls.

examTips: A short question may ask you to enlist the distinguishing characteristics of fungi. Include their way of feeding and the material in their cell walls.
A long question may ask you to describe all four Eukarya kingdoms. Give each kingdom its own clear point, using the correct terms for feeding, cell walls and body organisation.
For full marks, distinguish absorbing food from ingesting food: fungi absorb nutrients, while animals ingest food.
Use the textbook's examples accurately: yeast is a unicellular fungus; Amoeba and Paramecium are animal-like protists; mosses, ferns, conifers and flowering plants are plants.

explain.title: Protista
explain.body: Kingdom Protista includes eukaryotes which are unicellular or colonial or filamentous or simple multicellular. Simple multicellular means that they do not have multicellular sex organs. Plant-like protists are called algae, animal-like protists are called protozoans, and fungus-like protists absorb nutrients from decaying organic matter. For example, Amoeba and Paramecium are animal-like protists.

explain.title: Fungi
explain.body: Fungi are heterotrophic eukaryotes with cell walls made of chitin. They absorb food from decaying matter in their surroundings rather than ingesting it. Most fungi are multicellular, such as mushrooms and molds; a few, such as yeast, are unicellular. Penicillin is derived from the fungus Penicillium.

explain.title: Plantae
explain.body: Kingdom Plantae includes plants which are eukaryotic, multicellular organisms with cell walls made of cellulose. They are autotrophic and prepare food through photosynthesis. Examples include mosses, ferns, conifers and flowering plants.

explain.title: Animalia
explain.body: Kingdom Animalia includes animals which are eukaryotic, multicellular and heterotrophic. They develop from embryos, ingest food and digest it within their bodies. Vertebrates and invertebrates are included in this kingdom.

mistakes: Do not confuse absorption of food by fungi with ingestion of food by animals and animal-like protists.
Do not say that fungi have cellulose cell walls: the section says their walls are made of chitin.
Do not confuse the cell-wall materials: plants have cellulose walls, while fungi have chitin walls.
Do not describe all protists as the same kind of organism; the section includes plant-like, animal-like and fungus-like protists.
Do not omit that animals lack cell walls when giving the distinguishing characteristics of Animalia.
